newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil CVRD sale still tied-up in court.
newsitem.headline: Brazil CVRD sale still tied-up in court.

text.p: The Brazilian government skillfully smoothed away criticism in Congress to the sell-off of mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) but was ill-prepared for opposition in the courts, experts said Monday.

"The government underestimated the strength of the opposition and adopted a pushy, authoritative attitude. This is now being reflected in the behavior of the judiciary," said opposition Workers Party (PT) deputy Joao Fassarella.
"The government managed to control the dissatisfaction of deputies and senators by doing deals. But within the judiciary, the government's ability to horsetrade is more restricted."
On Monday it seemed unlikely the thrice-rescheduled auction of a controlling stake in CVRD would go ahead that day.

Delayed since April 29, the sell-off awaited the word of a judge in Brasilia who was due to rule on a key government petition that a host of injunctions against the sale should be judged by a single tribunal.

Justice Democrito Reinaldo of the Superior Court of Justice (STJ), the country's highest court for non-constitutional matters, is a friend of Vice President Marco Maciel but he has insisted he will not be swayed by political pressure.
Officials say they expected law suits, but not the deluge that poured in across Brazil in the hours before the hammer was due to come down on the world's largest iron ore exporter.
The government won over Congress by agreeing to use half the expected $5.0 billion in proceeds from Latin America's largest-ever privatization to invest in infrastructure.
It also set up a 200-million-real social investment fund and devised a mechanism by which the state will continue to have rights to 50 percent of any future discovered mineral wealth.
But its legion of lawyers flown around in four private jets proved insufficient to ensure the auction took place.

"All the waste of energy of the past days could have been avoided," wrote columnist Miriam Leitao in Sunday's Globo newspaper. "Underestimating the reaction to the sale of Vale, the government did not devise an efficient political strategy to unite its allies and conquer those still resisting the idea."
Jurists and political analysts said the government should have expected the judiciary to cause trouble.
"The judiciary is very reactionary. It is an elite with a tradition of independence," said political analyst Murillo Aragao of Brasilia-based consultants Arko Advice.
Aragao added that the judiciary was fighting a rearguard action against government attempts to reel in salaries and benefits. "The judiciary has it own agenda," he said.
But Aragao and other Brasilia watchers noted that the government had managed to quash 19 out of a total of 21 injunctions issued against the privatization.

The ruling from STJ justice Reinaldo has only assumed importance because of the government's inability to reverse one injunction granted by a Sao Paulo court at the request of some of the country's leading lawyers.
The lawyers argue the sale will "harm the nation's wealth".
"The government is taking on some very competent lawyers whose case is very well argued," said jurist Fernando Albino. "Sao Paulo is their real problem."
